stem: Let f : R -> R be defined by f(x) = x^2 - 4. Which of the following is true about f?

options.text: f is one-one but not onto
f is onto but not one-one
f is neither one-one nor onto

per_option_rationale.rationale: Failing to test f(2) = f(-2) = 0 (not one-one) and not checking that negative values like -5 have no pre-image (not onto), incorrectly concluding both properties hold.
Correctly identifying failure of one-one by missing the symmetry x vs -x, but then incorrectly claiming onto because the formula appears to range over all reals without checking the minimum value.

Concluding onto because 'every real number can be obtained from some x' without checking that f(x) = x^2 - 4 >= -4 always, so values below -4 are never reached; and concluding one-one fails which is correct but not the full picture.
Not one-one: f(2) = 0 = f(-2) but 2 not= -2. Not onto: f(x) = x^2 - 4 >= -4 for all real x, so no real x maps to, say, -5. Hence f is neither one-one nor onto.

explanation: f(x) = x^2 - 4 fails one-one because f(a) = f(-a) for all a, and fails onto because the minimum value -4 means no pre-image exists for any y < -4.

explanation_sections.punchline: A square function on all of R is always symmetric about 0 (not injective) and is bounded below (not surjective onto R).
explanation_sections.approach: State the property then contrast the confusable one. One-one (injective): distinct inputs give distinct outputs. Test f(2) = 0 and f(-2) = 0; since 2 != -2 but outputs match, f is NOT one-one. Onto (surjective): every element of the codomain R must have a pre-image. Since x^2 >= 0 always, f(x) = x^2 - 4 >= -4. Values like y = -5 have no solution x^2 = -1, so f is NOT onto. Both tests fail -> option 4.
explanation_sections.lesson: For f: R -> R with f(x) = x^2 + c, always check (i) even-function symmetry kills injectivity and (ii) minimum value kills surjectivity.
explanation_sections.timing: About 75 seconds. Test f(2) vs f(-2) first (40 sec), then check minimum of x^2-4 (20 sec). Trap: assuming all real y values are achievable because R is an infinite domain.
